Good afternoon class. This will be our last class before the break, and we have a three-week break coming up. I hope that during these weeks you have a chance to reflect on what we've learned because when we come back, we'll continue to build on the ideas we've covered so far. Today, I want to talk about meritocracy. The concept of meritocracy means that people should succeed based on their talent, ability, and hard work. In theory, this sounds like a good idea, and in fact, the school system is built around this idea—good students go to the best universities, which then leads to the best jobs.

However, I will show you today that there are many problems with meritocracy, and in reality, it's destroying American society. First, let me explain why America has one of the world’s most complicated admissions systems. In China, when you apply to university, you take the GACA exam, and then based on your test score, you get into a university. This is a system used by many countries. However, in America, multiple factors are considered: your transcript, standardized test scores like the SAT or TOEFL, extracurricular activities, teacher recommendation letters, and essays.

Now, let's go back to England in the 1600s. At this time, there was a major conflict between religious belief and the king. The king was head of the Anglican Church, which is the official church of England, with no significant differences from the Catholic Church except that in the Catholic Church, the head is the pope, while in the Anglican Church, it's the king. There were people called Protestants who believed there should be no pope or king; individuals should act as God directly by reading the Bible. This conflict led to wars and the solution was for the king to offer the Protestants a new place: America.

The Puritans, or dissenters, went to America to build their own theocracy, what they believed to be the New Jerusalem or paradise on earth. One core belief of the Protestants is that you must read the Bible to understand God's mind, making education and literacy divine imperatives. This led to the establishment of Harvard as a school to train ministers to study and spread the truth from the Bible.

Over time, as America became more wealthy, it also became less religious, and the Ivy League universities like Harvard, Yale, and Princeton, which were originally founded for religious purposes, became social clubs. These were places where the rich went to build cohesion rather than purely academic institutions.
